newsitem.title: Belgium: NATO tells military to start work on new force.
newsitem.headline: NATO tells military to start work on new force.

text.p: NATO countries, edging towards a new military commitment in Bosnia, instructed the military on Wednesday to start work on a possible new peace force when the mandate of the current mission expires in late December.

"The North Atlantic Council (NAC) has reached a provisional agreement to direct the military authorities to assess a range of options and to report the results by early next month," an alliance spokesman said.

He told reporters the alliance's 16 ambassadors agreed on the "political directives" asking the military to work on four possible options. These range from simply stopping a fresh outbreak of fighting to wide-ranging support for civilian reconstruction efforts.

He added that the policy-making NAC, comprising of the ambassadors of NATO states, would hold talks on Thursday and Friday with non-alliance states serving in the current Implementation Force (IFOR) before finalising the instructions.
"We want to involve non-alliance participating members at an earlier stage than for IFOR," said one senior alliance official.
NATO countries first publicly acknowledged it would be necessary to keep several thousand troops in Bosnia next year at an informal meeting in Bergen, Norway at the end of September.
But since then they have quibbled over the exact language of the instructions to the military who want to push on with planning for the follow-on force.

NATO officials, reflecting the high degree of sensitivity of the issue ahead of the U.S. presidential election, stressed no decision on replacing the 55,000-strong alliance led force had yet been taken.
"There is no commitment by NATO to any particular course of action, this is just contingency planning. It does not mean we have taken a decision to be in Bosnia in 1997," added the official.

However, all countries now accept such a force will be necessary if the Dayton peace accords, policed by the IFOR, are to last beyond the end of the year and to give emerging civilian institutions time to take root.

Alliance sources said the length of mandate of any new force had yet to be agreed, with the United States pushing for one year and the Europeans favouring a commitment to two. The exact link with the international community's High Representative in Bosnia Carl Bildt also had to be determined.
The military, keen to finalise planning for any new force, have been told to report back on how many troops would be needed to implement any of the following four options:
-- total withdrawal of the existing force in line with present political instructions
-- a deterrence force limited to preventing a fresh outbreak of fighting
-- a deterrence force with a mandate to increase stability and to give limited help to civilian reconstruction efforts
-- a deterrence force with a mandate to increase stability and give wide-ranging support to civilian reconstruction efforts.
